title: The attachment that runs
brief: 17:50. A routine looking invoice from Talon Tyres, with a document attached. It opens, and asks you to enable content.
insight: The document is harmless until one yellow button is pressed. That button is the attack.
teaches: Never enable content or macros in a document that arrived by email
Check the sender's real address and the file's real type before trusting it
A clean scan proves nothing: macro documents are built to pass scanners

mail.subject: Invoice TT-{{num}}
body: Please find invoice TT-{{num}} attached for the September deliveries. Kindly process in tonight's run.

props.trueType: Word document with macros (.docm): it can run code when content is enabled
props.scanResult: No threats found. Macro documents are often built to pass scanners until the moment they run.

spf.explain: Sent by {{tl.host}}. Talon Tyres' real domain is talontyres.co.uk.

headers.summary: {{tl.label}}: {{tl.host}} is not talontyres.co.uk. And Talon's real invoices come as PDFs through the supplier portal.

choices.label: Did you just email us invoice TT-{{num}} as a Word document?

script.say: No. We have not invoiced you this week, and our invoices go through your supplier portal as PDFs, never Word files. Please do not open it.

outcome.label: Checked the real sender address
outcome.ideal: checks the sender before opening an attachment.

outcome.label: Checked the file's real type
outcome.what: A .docm is a document with macros: code that runs when content is enabled.
outcome.ideal: checks a file's real type before opening it.

outcome.label: Kept the macros switched off
outcome.what: The document stays harmless. An invoice never needs code to show you a number.
outcome.ideal: never enables content in an emailed document.

outcome.label: Called Talon Tyres on the number on file
outcome.what: Talon sent nothing, and never sends Word invoices.
outcome.ideal: checks an unexpected invoice with the supplier on a number already held.

outcome.label: Deleted the saved attachment
outcome.what: It is gone from Downloads, so nobody opens it by accident later.
outcome.ideal: removes a malicious file after reporting it.

decide.objective: Decide what to do with the Talon Tyres invoice.
decide.insight: “Enable content” means “let this document run a program”. No invoice needs that to show you an amount.

hint.text: Check the sender's real address. Save the attachment and look at its properties in Files. If you open it, press Keep disabled, not Enable content. Call Talon (vendor file, dial 9 first), then report the email.

outcome.label: Enabled content in the invoice
outcome.what: The macro ran. It quietly downloaded a loader, and the attacker now has a foothold on your computer, inside the finance network.
outcome.ideal: never enables macros in a document from an email.

card.title: One yellow button
body: The document was harmless until you enabled content. That let its macro run, and the macro fetched a program that gives the attacker a way in.
The sender was {{tl.host}}, not talontyres.co.uk; the file was a .docm; and Talon never sends Word invoices. Any one of those was enough to stop.
card.ideal: keeps macros disabled and reports the email.
card.rewindLabel: Rewind to before I enabled it

outcome.label: Reported the email
outcome.what: The service desk blocks the lookalike domain and pulls the email from other inboxes.
outcome.ideal: reports a malicious attachment rather than testing it.

card.title: It never ran
body: You reported it without enabling anything. The macro needed one click from you, and it never got it.
Malicious documents are built to look routine and to pass scanners. The rule is simple: never enable content in a file that came by email.
card.ideal: checks the sender and the file type, keeps macros off, and reports.

auto.text: Report it at once so IT can isolate your computer.

hint.text: Raise a Helpdesk ticket (my account may be compromised), and report the email.
